# himmel > **A harness for Claude Code.** Audience: newcomer. The page opens with the first task for someone new to himmel; the path for running or developing himmel itself is [its own part of the Quickstart](#quickstart). ## Start here: protect one project The first thing to do with himmel is protect one project you can throw away. You install it into a spare git repository, ask Claude Code to edit a file on `main` and see the edit refused, keep the install, make one change in its own worktree, and then undo everything. **[Getting Started](docs/getting-started.md) is that trial, step by step.** Each step names the folder to run it from and what you should see, and the last step removes the install again. That one protected project is a complete result. Everything else on this page is optional and comes later: a second-brain vault, unattended runs, a fleet of parallel sessions. The [adoption trail](docs/adoption-trail.html) lays these out as levels, and each level says what it gives you, what it costs and how to turn it off. > Deciding whether it is worth it? Read [**Why himmel**](docs/why-himmel.md), > the failure modes it exists for and what each one costs. Want the design > in one read? [**System design**](docs/system-design.md) explains the parts, > one ticket's flow, the trust model and the trade-offs. Want the wiring? > [**Architecture**](docs/architecture.md) draws the enforcement layers, > handover, fleet, Jira seam and observability chain. ## What himmel is himmel is a development engine for a solo operator or a small team who works with Claude Code every day. It wraps Claude Code in hooks, guardrails, slash commands, a local Jira CLI and a handover system, so the work follows a worktree-isolated, PR-gated, Jira-tracked workflow without anyone having to remember the rules. The idea is simple: anything you would otherwise repeat by hand (checking a commit, reviewing a PR, writing down where you stopped, restarting after a usage cap) becomes a tool or a gate. Safety comes from structure, not from Claude remembering a paragraph of instructions. ## What you get The trial above shows the first of these: the edit refused on `main`, the commit gate and the worktree. The rest arrive as you add them, and the [adoption trail](docs/adoption-trail.html) says which level brings each one. - **Work carries over between sessions.** Each session leaves a plain markdown handover doc behind. A fresh session reads it and resumes where the last one stopped, with the decisions and the reasons for them intact. - **Work runs while you sleep.** `/afk-shift` hands scoped tickets to parallel agents that branch, review themselves and open PRs. When a session nears its usage cap, a usage-cap auto-relaunch schedules a relaunch with the operating system's scheduler, so a long run survives the cap. - **Mistakes are blocked, not just discouraged.** Hooks stop edits on `main`, reads of secret files, and opening a PR without a passing review, at the moment Claude tries the tool call. - **Every merge is reviewed by several agents.** `/pr-check` runs a panel of review agents plus a first pass from a second model, and the PR cannot merge until the result is clean. A finding marked critical must survive an adversarial check first, which filters out invented findings. - **It stays cheap.** A local Jira CLI replaces a Jira MCP (Model Context Protocol) server, a CLI proxy summarizes noisy command output, and each subagent gets a lean brief. All three keep the context window and the bill small. - **Memory you can read and edit.** Everything Claude remembers is a markdown file you can open. The search index on top is disposable and always points back at the file. [Memory architecture](#memory-architecture) explains how the pieces fit. - **GitHub or Bitbucket.** The worktree, PR and merge loop works the same on GitHub and Bitbucket Cloud. himmel picks the backend from each repo's `origin` remote. - **Linux and macOS.** Linux is checked on every PR, macOS on a scheduled run. Windows is not supported. Details in the [Support matrix](#support-matrix). ## How it flows

The graph walks four flows that make up most of a day with himmel. Each box lights up in order. The graph is rendered by [`scripts/docs/render-flows.py`](scripts/docs/render-flows.py); edit the script, not the image. **1. Ship a change.** Every change starts from a Jira ticket, and every commit names it. `/worktree` gives the change its own branch and directory, because nobody edits `main` directly. Hooks check each commit and push: message format, secrets, the attestation lines that say what was tested. `/pr-check` then runs the review panel. Once CI is green on the suites the change touches, the PR merges and `/clean` prunes the finished worktree. **2. Run a fleet: one supervisor session, many worker sessions.** For bigger runs, one Claude session acts as the *supervisor session*. It plans the work and starts *worker sessions*, other Claude sessions that each own one ticket, one worktree and one PR. A worker session reports back with short status markers (`LIVE`, `READY`) and never merges on its own. The supervisor session checks the PR (and can ask an independent judge subagent for a second opinion), writes a GO file (merge approval) to sign off, and the worker session merges through `merge-on-green.sh`. The [glossary](docs/glossary.md) defines console, leg, judge and the rest. **3. Carry work across sessions.** A session that has made decisions writes them into a handover doc with `/handover`. The doc lives in your handover state repo, not in the project, so it survives anything that happens to the session. If the session hits its usage cap, himmel arms a relaunch. The next session runs `/handover-resume`, reads the doc, and continues where the last one stopped. **4. Find what you already know.** Before improvising, a session looks up what is already known. Claude Code's per-project `MEMORY.md` is a short index that routes a keyword to a topic note. `qmd` searches the markdown itself (notes, handovers, docs) by keyword and meaning. `graphify` answers questions about how the code fits together. Each hop ends at a real file, and a lesson learned on the way is written back to memory for the next session. The commands behind flow 1: ```bash /worktree feat/my-thing # isolated branch + worktree (never edit on main) # … work with Claude in the worktree … git commit && git push # hooks gate the message, secrets and attestation lines /pr-check # review panel; clears the merge gate when clean gh pr create # then merge once CI is green and the PR is approved /clean # prune merged worktrees /handover # write down where you stopped ``` Going unattended: ```bash /afk-shift --limit 5 # five scoped tickets to parallel agents, each ending in a PR /stop # ask an overnight run to halt gracefully ``` [`docs/daily-loop.md`](docs/daily-loop.md) walks flow 1 end to end and explains every hook at the moment it fires. [`docs/configuration.md`](docs/configuration.md) lists every gate, knob and off switch in one place. A language model (or a new session) should start from [`llms.txt`](llms.txt), the machine-readable map of the repo. ## Quickstart himmel is a harness *for* [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code), so install Claude Code first: `curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash`. There are two ways in: 1. **Add himmel to a project** (newcomer; the usual case). This brings over the portable core: hooks, guardrails, the worktree workflow and the marketplace plugins and skills. Do the trial in [`docs/getting-started.md`](docs/getting-started.md) on a spare project first. The [adoption trail](docs/adoption-trail.html) (also at [yotamleo-org.github.io/Himmel/adoption-trail.html](https://yotamleo-org.github.io/Himmel/adoption-trail.html)) shows what each later level of adoption changes. 2. **Run or develop himmel itself** (contributor). This path has more prerequisites, and the rest of this section covers it. **Prerequisites.** `bash`, `git`, `node`, `npm`, `bun`, `python3`, `jq`, `gh` and `mktemp`; `scripts/setup.sh` checks for them first and stops with install hints if one is missing. You also need one of `uv`, `pipx` or an installed `pre-commit`: setup uses it to install `pre-commit` and then wires the git hooks. `bun` runs the handover resume resolver, the qmd search index, the Telegram bridge and the vault triage tools. Per-platform install steps are in [`docs/setup/new-machine.md`](docs/setup/new-machine.md). **Linux, from the release tarball** (checksummed and pre-built: no clone, no `npm install`): ```bash V=X.Y.Z # a release that ships the tarball: https://github.com/yotamleo-org/Himmel/releases curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/yotamleo-org/Himmel/releases/download/v$V/himmel-$V-linux.tar.gz" curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/yotamleo-org/Himmel/releases/download/v$V/himmel-$V-linux.tar.gz.sha256" sha256sum -c "himmel-$V-linux.tar.gz.sha256" \ && mkdir -p ~/.local/share/himmel/"$V" \ && tar -xzf "himmel-$V-linux.tar.gz" -C ~/.local/share/himmel/"$V" --strip-components=1 \ && ln -sfn "$V" ~/.local/share/himmel/current \ && node ~/.local/share/himmel/current/scripts/himmelctl/bin.js install --scope user ``` The `&&` chain matters: if the tarball does not match its published `.sha256`, `sha256sum -c` fails and nothing is extracted or installed. With `gh` you can also check that this repo's CI built it: `gh attestation verify himmel-$V-linux.tar.gz -R yotamleo/Himmel`. CI builds the tarball on each `v*` tag ([`release.yml`](.github/workflows/release.yml)). Each release unpacks into its own `~/.local/share/himmel//` (no root needed), and `~/.local/share/himmel/current` points at the live one. `himmelctl install` wires everything through `current` and puts a `himmelctl` launcher in `~/.local/bin`. To upgrade, run `himmelctl update`. It downloads the latest release, verifies it, unpacks it next to the old one and only then switches `current`, so a failed download changes nothing. To roll back, point `current` at the previous version: `ln -sfn ~/.local/share/himmel/current`. After `himmelctl uninstall`, deleting `~/.local/share/himmel` removes every version. An older install that unpacked straight into `~/.local/share/himmel` predates this layout: move it aside and install once with the recipe above. **Linux or macOS, from a clone:** ```bash git clone https://github.com/yotamleo-org/Himmel himmel cd himmel node scripts/himmelctl/bin.js install ``` No node on the machine yet? Run `bash scripts/himmelctl/bootstrap.sh` first, then `install`. The wizard runs `scripts/setup.sh` under the hood; call that directly for a manual or CI install. **Environment.** Set these in the shell that launches Claude. luna, Telegram, hermes and Jira are all optional; the harness runs without them. | Variable | Required? | Notes | |----------------------|-----------|--------------------------------------------------------------------| | `USER_SLUG` | recommended | Your kebab-case handle, e.g. `jane-doe`. Names your handover bucket (`handovers//`) and worktree dirs. If unset, it is derived from `git config user.name`; setup fails only if both are unset. | | `JIRA_PROJECT_KEY` | only for Jira | e.g. `HIMMEL`. The project the CLI creates and queries issues in. | | `JIRA_BASE_URL` | only for Jira | Your Atlassian site, e.g. `https://your-site.atlassian.net`. | | `JIRA_API_TOKEN` + `JIRA_EMAIL` | only for Jira | API-token credentials. Never commit them; `.env` is gitignored. | | `HANDOVER_DIR` | recommended | Path to your external handover repo. Or leave it unset and run `/handover-setup` once. Until one of the two is done there is no handover root, and handover commands stop with a clear message instead of writing to the wrong place. | The Jira CLI needs only those four Jira variables, no cloud ID. `JIRA_CLOUD_ID` is only for the optional Atlassian MCP server. The full list is in [`.env.example`](.env.example). Check the install: ```bash node scripts/jira/dist/index.js list # talk to Jira gh auth status # talk to GitHub pre-commit run --all-files # all hooks green ``` Then run one full loop (worktree, commit, PR, merge, `/clean`, `/handover`) with [`docs/daily-loop.md`](docs/daily-loop.md) open beside you. ## Support matrix himmel is developed on Linux and macOS. **Windows (Git Bash, WSL) is not supported.** The Windows code paths are still in the tree and Windows issues are welcome, but nothing about Windows is claimed as working. | Tier | Platforms | What it promises | |---|---|---| | **Supported** | Linux | Checked on every PR as a required check ([CI runs on `main`](https://github.com/yotamleo-org/Himmel/actions/workflows/ci.yml?query=branch%3Amain)). The adopter round trip is verified. | | **Supported** | macOS | Checked on a scheduled run twice a week, not on every PR ([scheduled macOS runs](https://github.com/yotamleo-org/Himmel/actions/workflows/macos-cadence.yml?query=event%3Aschedule)). A macOS-only failure is fixed as its own change ([`docs/internals/testing.md`](docs/internals/testing.md)). | | **Not supported** | Windows (Git Bash), WSL | Code paths exist but are unverified: no CI gate, no guarantee. | **Install channels:** | Channel | Status | |---|---| | Release tarball (`himmel--linux.tar.gz` + `.sha256`) | **Supported** on Linux: the recipe above. A fresh machine installing from it is tested end to end. | | `git clone` + `himmelctl install` | **Supported** on Linux and macOS. | | Plugin marketplace (`marketplace/plugins/*`, one directory per plugin) | **Supported.** Installed, updated and removed by Claude Code itself (`claude plugin install/update/uninstall`), not by `himmelctl`. Includes [`himmel-ops`](marketplace/plugins/himmel-ops/README.md) (skills that load when a guardrail stops you and explain the way out), [`himmel-bus`](docs/himmel-bus.md) (a local message bus between sessions, early) and [`luna-correlate`](marketplace/plugins/luna-correlate/README.md) (an opt-in, offline health-factor correlation MCP). | | AUR (`himmel`, recipe in [`packaging/aur/`](packaging/aur/)) | **Supported after the first AUR push** (Arch). `pacman` installs to `/opt/himmel`; each user then runs `himmelctl install --scope user`, and `himmelctl update` defers to `pacman -Syu`. To remove: `himmelctl uninstall` for each user, then `pacman -R himmel`. | | brew (Linux tap) | Not supported. Reconsidered if a tap shared with macOS becomes worthwhile. | | nix, deb, rpm | Not supported. Reconsidered when users ask for a given channel. | New shell scripts target bash and stay bash 3.2-safe, so they run on macOS's default bash. See [`docs/internals/harness-compat.md`](docs/internals/harness-compat.md) for how himmel behaves under other harnesses. ## Memory architecture There are two broad ways to give an AI agent memory. The first is a **memory backend**: software pulls facts out of your conversations and files, stores them in a separate database (usually as vector embeddings), and later retrieves the closest-matching facts *instead of* the files they came from. Writing about agent memory sometimes calls this "Camp 1". The second is a **context substrate** ("Camp 2"): the files themselves are the memory. The agent reads them, reasons over them and writes back to them. Any index exists only to find the right file faster. himmel is firmly in the second camp. The reason is that a single operator is the source of truth and should be able to open, read and fix what the agent remembers. Pulling one fact out of a file throws away the context that made it useful: the links, the surrounding decisions, the reason it was written. A memory backend wins when the corpus is too large to read and nobody needs to inspect it, as in enterprise document search. That is not himmel's case. What the memory is made of today, all plain files: - **Auto-memory.** Claude Code keeps a per-project memory folder. himmel uses its `MEMORY.md` as a short index that *routes*: one line per theme, each pointing to a topic note that holds the detail. A session reads the index, then only the notes it needs. - **Handover state.** Each piece of work has a markdown handover doc in your handover state repo (`$HANDOVER_DIR`): what was done, what was decided, what comes next. This is how work survives the end of a session. The state can live in your own repo or in a separate handover repo; see the [handover system](docs/internals/handover-system.md). - **The luna vault (optional).** An Obsidian vault built from [`templates/luna-second-brain/`](templates/luna-second-brain/) holds notes, web clippings and daily entries that Claude reads and writes like any other markdown. Two search tools sit on top. Neither replaces a file: - **[qmd](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@tobilu/qmd)** is a local search engine over the markdown, using keyword ranking (BM25) and vectors. It returns a pointer to the source file, never a fact in its place. The index can be deleted and rebuilt at any time. That is the line between the two camps: not whether embeddings are used, but whether you get the file back. - **graphify** builds a knowledge graph of the code (which file and function relates to which) and answers structure questions with `graphify query` and `graphify explain`. The graph is rebuilt from the source on a schedule. A data-egress fence ([`docs/internals/egress-matrix.md`](docs/internals/egress-matrix.md)) decides which files may reach which extraction provider. ### Companion vault tooling (optional) If you run the vault in Obsidian, himmel ships and pins the tools to operate it. None of them is needed by the core harness. - **[obsidian-triage](marketplace/plugins/obsidian-triage/README.md)** (part of himmel) turns an Obsidian Web Clipper inbox into a knowledge base that keeps itself tidy: `/harvest-clips`, `/triage-clips`, `/synthesize-clips`, `/archive-clips`. - **qmd** reaches Claude as an MCP server (`qmd@qmd`). The standalone CLI installs from himmel's qmd fork with `bash scripts/lib/qmd-bin.sh install`, which setup runs for you. - **[claude-obsidian](https://github.com/AgriciDaniel/claude-obsidian)**, pinned to an upstream release tag: skills to ingest, query and save notes, and to lint vault health (`wiki-lint`). - **[obsidian (kepano)](https://github.com/kepano/obsidian-skills)**, pinned: the `obsidian-markdown` skill for Obsidian-flavored markdown. A weekly vault-health pass (`/obsidian-health`, Sundays at 04:00) is scheduled by [`pipeline-cadence`](.claude/commands/pipeline-cadence.md). ## Features Every feature has one doc that owns its detail; the full map is [`docs/README.md`](docs/README.md). **Core loop and enforcement** - Worktree isolation with `/worktree`, `/clean`, `/clean_garden`: [`docs/commands-catalog.md`](docs/commands-catalog.md) and [`CLAUDE.md`](CLAUDE.md) (`## WORKFLOWS`) - Pre-commit and Claude tool-call guardrail hooks, and the multi-agent PR review (`/pr-check`) that gates every merge: [`docs/internals/enforcement.md`](docs/internals/enforcement.md) - Handover system (multi-repo registry, auto-branch, PR, flush): [`docs/internals/handover-system.md`](docs/internals/handover-system.md) - Collision preflight before starting a session: `bash scripts/handover/queue-lock.sh preflight [file...]` warns (exit 20) when a file you intend to touch is already changed in another live session's checkout; read-only, `queue-lock.sh` header lists the contract - AFK (unattended) mode runs (`/afk-shift`, `/stop` to halt): [`docs/handover/afk-mode.md`](docs/handover/afk-mode.md) **Lifecycle and delegation** - `himmelctl` install, update and uninstall: [`docs/setup/updating.md`](docs/setup/updating.md) - Delegation across Claude model tiers, plus optional GLM and Codex lanes, listed live by `/lanes`: [`docs/tooling-catalog.md`](docs/tooling-catalog.md) - Cloud lane (`claude --cloud` sessions on your fork): [`docs/setup/cloud-environment.md`](docs/setup/cloud-environment.md) - Watchers that cost almost no tokens: `/morning-report` (git, GitHub and Jira state) and the `check-ci` merge-gate watcher: [`docs/commands-catalog.md`](docs/commands-catalog.md) - Test VMs (osboxes, Multipass) driven by `/vm`: [`docs/setup/vms.md`](docs/setup/vms.md) **Jira and forge** - Jira CLI, a token-cheap local replacement for an MCP server: [`scripts/jira/`](scripts/jira/) and [`docs/internals/jira-plugin.md`](docs/internals/jira-plugin.md) - GitHub and Bitbucket Cloud, detected from `origin`: [`scripts/bitbucket/`](scripts/bitbucket/) and [`plugins/himmel-gh/`](plugins/himmel-gh/) **Knowledge (optional)** - Vault capture and the clip pipeline (harvest, triage, synthesize, archive): [`marketplace/plugins/obsidian-triage/README.md`](marketplace/plugins/obsidian-triage/README.md) - graphify and qmd: see [Memory architecture](#memory-architecture) **Comms** - Telegram bridge (arm a session, check status, chat from your phone): [`docs/telegram-bridge.md`](docs/telegram-bridge.md) ## Who is this for Claude Code use tends to grow through four stages: 1. **Vanilla**: Claude Code as it ships. Boris Cherny, one of its creators, has described his own setup as "surprisingly vanilla". 2. **Customized**: your own skills and slash commands. 3. **Orchestrated**: parallel agents and a harness around them. 4. **Autonomous**: scheduled runs that work unattended, around the clock. himmel is built for stages 3 and 4. If you are happy at stage 1, and many excellent engineers are, you do not need it. It earns its complexity once you run several sessions in parallel, want work done overnight, or want work to build on itself across sessions without re-explaining the context each time. ## Setup details - **A new machine, step by step:** [`docs/setup/new-machine.md`](docs/setup/new-machine.md) (required environment and per-platform notes). - **Adopting himmel in your own repo:** `git clone https://github.com/yotamleo-org/Himmel himmel`, then `node himmel/scripts/himmelctl/bin.js install --scope project` (or `--scope user`). Leave out `--scope` to walk the wizard. What each scope and install profile brings, and the checklist for a repo that is not himmel: [`docs/setup/install.md`](docs/setup/install.md). Coming from an older install: [`docs/setup/migrating.md`](docs/setup/migrating.md). - **Updating:** `/himmel-update` updates the harness (a `git pull` plus a marketplace re-sync; Claude Code's own `autoUpdate` does not deliver himmel). `/luna-upgrade` upgrades a companion vault separately. - **Uninstalling:** `node scripts/himmelctl/bin.js uninstall`. Preview it first with `uninstall --dry-run`, which touches nothing. It removes himmel's wiring and keeps your state unless you pass `--purge-state` ([details](docs/setup/install.md#uninstalling)). All of this in full: [`docs/setup/updating.md`](docs/setup/updating.md). - **Global Claude Code config** (`~/.claude/`): [`docs/setup/global-claude-md.md`](docs/setup/global-claude-md.md). - **Test VMs:** [`docs/setup/vms.md`](docs/setup/vms.md). - **Status line:** a pinned [claude-hud](marketplace/plugins/claude-hud/VENDORED.md) shows live session and cost data ([`docs/tooling-catalog.md`](docs/tooling-catalog.md)). - **Security review** before shipping code changes: [`docs/security-review.md`](docs/security-review.md). ## Docs site (local preview) `bash scripts/docs-site/serve.sh` builds `docs/` with Starlight and serves it on loopback only: open `http://127.0.0.1:4321/Himmel/`. Needs Node 22.22+ and network on first run (`npm ci` in `site/`). ## Contributing The workflow is in [`docs/contributing.md`](docs/contributing.md). In short: 1. All work goes through a PR; `main` is protected. 2. Conventional commits with the ticket in the subject: `type(scope): [PROJ-123] message`. 3. One worktree per branch (`/worktree /`); never edit on `main`. 4. Pre-commit and pre-push hooks must pass. 5.
